messages.subject: Sample independent variable given dependent variable values
parts:
I'm sure this is really simple, but I can't figure it out...

Say I have the standard linear regression model from Section 6.1 of the guide. I can do these successfully:
1. Provide the model with x and y values, and get samples from alpha and beta (the regression parameters).
2. Provide the model with an additional vector of x values, and output additional y values in the "generated quantities" block (posterior predictive check).
3. Change the model, so that x is a distribution. This allows me to output the posterior of x.

However, what I would like to do is a mixture of 2 and 3:
Provide the model with an additional vector of y values (y_test), and output the posterior of x (x_test), corresponding to the additional y values.

Is there a recommended way of doing this?

I tried adding a new sampling statement (below), but this modified all the other parameters. It might work if I could "fix" alpha, beta and sigma in this statement...
y_test ~ normal(alpha + beta * x_test, sigma);

Thanks in advance.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sample independent variable given dependent variable values
parts:
You need to think in terms of inference for unknowns.
When you predict new y-tilde given new x-tilde, you
are using the model in its forward (generative) direction.
In order to infer the x from y, you need to invert everything
Bayesian style. In Stan terms, this means defining a joint
distribution p(y, x, alpha, beta), which you've done if you've
given x a distribution, then you need to do inference on
x-tilde given y-tilde and alpha and beta. To do that in Stan,
you need to declare the x-tilde as parameters unless you
can analytically figure out p(x | y, alpha, beta) [which is
sometimes possible for joint models such as Gaussian
processes].

- Bob

y_new is missing the intercept term: alpha. Unless that's intentional.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sample independent variable given dependent variable values
parts:
Unless you are trying to build in a measurement error
model, you want to replace this:

> x_dist ~ normal(x, sigma_x);
> y ~ normal(alpha + beta * x_dist, sigma);
>
> // Replicate the model, so we can sample x_tilde, given y_tilde.
> y_tilde ~ normal(alpha + beta * x_tilde, sigma);

with

parameters {
real mu;
...

model {
x ~ normal(mu, sigma_x); // need a new parameter mu for this and a new
x_tilde ~ normal(mu, sigma_x); // new x's distributed same way

y ~ normal(alpha + beta * x, sigma); // y's given by regression
y_tilde ~ normal(alpha + beta * x_tilde, sigma); // new y's done same way

If you're building measurement error to x, then you need to add another
level.

In this model, I don't think x_tilde and y_tilde will affect
estimates of alpha, beta, or sigma (but x_tilde will affect
mu and sigma_x).

- Bob

Ok, that worked pretty well!
I'm still a bit confused, so I'll explain my thoughts...

Now, x and x_tilde come from the same distribution N(mu, sigma_x). This is what fixed the problem.
y and y_tilde also come from a common distribution, which makes sense.

For (x, y), we are providing data for both x and y, and the "free" parameters are alpha, beta and sigma. I'm using the default uniform priors for these, so they are free to fall where they may.
However, for (x_tilde, y_tilde), we are only providing y_tilde. Since there is one less constraint (no x_tilde data), there will be minimal effect on alpha, beta and sigma.
So, alpha, beta and sigma are more influenced by (x, y) than (x_tilde, y_tilde).
And, x_tilde falls out as desired.

Is this correct?

My next step is to perform some conditional posterior predictions.
For example, if I now have two predictors, x1 and x2, and at some point I learn the true value of x1, what is the subsequent posterior of x2?
I think I can figure this out, but any tips would be appreciated.

Thanks!

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sample independent variable given dependent variable values
parts:
> On Aug 12, 2016, at 12:15 AM, Paul <pwmor...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Ok, that worked pretty well!
Glad to hear it.
> I'm still a bit confused, so I'll explain my thoughts...

This stuff's all very confusing the first time around until you
get the hang of thinking in terms of the marginal distributions
of the things you're interested in and can work all the algebra
out in your head (I'm still counting on my fingers; Michael
and Andrew do this stuff at the snap of a finger).

>
> Now, x and x_tilde come from the same distribution N(mu, sigma_x). This is what fixed the problem.
Not just that. It's that
> y and y_tilde also come from a common distribution, which makes sense.

They come from a common distribution only conditioned on alpha, beta,
sigma and x and x_tilde.
> For (x, y), we are providing data for both x and y, and the "free" parameters are alpha, beta and sigma. I'm using the default uniform priors for these, so they are free to fall where they may.

That's not the right way to think about it. The right
way to think about uniform priors is that they put a ton of
probability mass out in the tails --- they're not uniform in
the way most people think. That is, they put a million times
more weight on a value being between 1 million and 2 million
than they put on the value being between 0 and 1. Andrew's
written extensively on this [see the manual for citations to papers,
or check out BDA]. This is why we don't even like those hacked
"flat(tish)" priors from BUGS, such as gamma(0.001, 0.001)
or normal(0, 1000). We almost always have some notion of the
scale of the results before we start.
> However, for (x_tilde, y_tilde), we are only providing y_tilde. Since there is one less constraint (no x_tilde data), there will be minimal effect on alpha, beta and sigma.

The reason is just that if you look at the posterior

p(alpha, beta, sigma | y, x)

without x_tilde involved at all, and compare it to the marginal
posterior

p(alpha, beta, sigma | y, x, x_tilde)

you get from

p(alpha, beta, sigma, y_tilde | y, x, x_tilde)

then they are the same. Warning: this isn't the case for
every "missing data" model (though that term is vague, so you
have to be careful with definitions).

> So, alpha, beta and sigma are more influenced by (x, y) than (x_tilde, y_tilde).
> And, x_tilde falls out as desired.
>
> Is this correct?
>
> My next step is to perform some conditional posterior predictions.
> For example, if I now have two predictors, x1 and x2, and at some point I learn the true value of x1, what is the subsequent posterior of x2?
> I think I can figure this out, but any tips would be appreciated.

You just need to fix x1, then you can do inference on x2. In general,
in Bayesian models, you set up a joint distribution and you can
then do inference on whichever variables you want given observations
of the others.

The manual chapter on missing data is what you want to look at for
how to code this up in Stan. It's easier in BUGS/JAGS as they just
let you pass in the equivalent of R's NA wherever you want and figure
out all the coding internally (the benefit of restricting your attention
to acyclic directed graphical models).

- Bob

I would recommend Gelman and Hill's regression book as the
next step. I found it very hard to jump into BDA myself because
it presupposes you have a very good grasp of math stats before
you start. But once you're ready to read it, it's awesome.
Peter Hoff's book is nice, too, if you're comfortable with calc
and linear algebra, but not with math stats.

> > Now, x and x_tilde come from the same distribution N(mu, sigma_x). This is what fixed the problem.
>

>

> sigma and x and x_tilde.
>
> > For (x, y), we are providing data for both x and y, and the "free" parameters are alpha, beta and sigma. I'm using the default uniform priors for these, so they are free to fall where they may.
>
> That's not the right way to think about it. The right
> way to think about uniform priors is that they put a ton of

> or normal(0, 1000). We almost always have some notion of the

We have recommendations on our wiki for priors

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations

and also in the manual regression chapter. In particular, we do *not*
recommend hard upper and lower bounds other than for parameters
that are physically constrained (like for bernoulli or binomial
parameters which must be in (0, 1), or scale parameters which
must be in (0, inf)).

> I'm thinking of my x and x_tilde distributions, which are currently normally distributed. The x and x_tilde data I'm creating is randomly distributed over the range [-5, 5], so a normal distribution doesn't seem appropriate. Should I specify a uniform distribution with these bounds?

This is a case where it would be appropriate because it's the
true model. But you probalby just want to simulate with normal(0, 2)
or something rather than uniform(-5, 5).

> > However, for (x_tilde, y_tilde), we are only providing y_tilde. Since there is one less constraint (no x_tilde data), there will be minimal effect on alpha, beta and sigma.
>
> The reason is just that if you look at the posterior
>
> p(alpha, beta, sigma | y, x)
>
> without x_tilde involved at all, and compare it to the marginal
> posterior
>
> p(alpha, beta, sigma | y, x, x_tilde)
>
> you get from
>

> every "missing data" model (though that term is vague, so you
> have to be careful with definitions).
>
> Ok, I'll need to think about this.

This is the kind of thing that BDA assumes you're going to
be comfortable doing.

> > So, alpha, beta and sigma are more influenced by (x, y) than (x_tilde, y_tilde).
> > And, x_tilde falls out as desired.
> >
> > Is this correct?
> >
> > My next step is to perform some conditional posterior predictions.
> > For example, if I now have two predictors, x1 and x2, and at some point I learn the true value of x1, what is the subsequent posterior of x2?
> > I think I can figure this out, but any tips would be appreciated.
>
> You just need to fix x1, then you can do inference on x2. In general,
> in Bayesian models, you set up a joint distribution and you can
> then do inference on whichever variables you want given observations
> of the others.
>
> That worked ok, when I fix x1_tilde.
>
> If I don't fix x1_tilde (both x1_tilde and x2_tilde are parameters), I'm not sure what to expect.
> Will I get the joint distribution of x1_tilde and x2_tilde, given y_tilde (and the other parameters)?
Exactly. That's always what you get given a joint distribution.
> Then, the modes of the x1_tilde and x2_tilde posterior marginals would indicate the values most likely to have generated the given y_tilde?

"Most likely" is not a Bayesian concept because it has zero measure
(no probability mass). The marginal posterior means give you the
Bayesian point estimate that minimizes expected square error. The
posterior mode doesn't have an interpretation in and of itself because
it depends on parameterization. I wrote a case study for this:

http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/mle-params.html

- Bob
